description: Somos un equipo de desarrolladores y entusiastas de la ciencia que crea un simulador de misión para astronautas junior. Usamos datos abiertos de la NASA para que niños y jóvenes vivan una misión espacial completa: planificar, tomar decisiones y ver las consecuencias, todo desde el navegador.
summary:
Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to radiation, microgravity, isolation, and a closed hostile environment — all of which can trigger immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and mental health problems. On missions to Mars, Earth support can be minutes or hours away, so crew must detect and act on their own health changes.

H.A.L.O. is a browser-based health monitoring app that ingests vitals from a simulated Astroskin-style wearable, evaluates them against NASA-sourced thresholds, and gives the astronaut plain-language guidance (what the value means, what to do next). An integrated AI assistant correlates the crew member’s vitals with their habitat context (ISS, transit, Moon base, Mars base) — radiation dose, gravity, isolation — and simultaneously alerts Earth with the expected communication delay. It is designed to be usable by non-clinicians under stress: short sentences, verb-first instructions, color-coded states (green / yellow / red), and no diagnostic language.
details:
Problem. On a Mars-class mission, crew members bear most of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves. Radiation dose accumulates silently; bone density drops ~1–1.5% per month in microgravity; cardiovascular adaptation causes orthostatic events on gravity changes; isolation degrades sleep and mood. A non-clinician astronaut needs a tool that measures, interprets, and prescribes action — without requiring medical expertise.

What H.A.L.O. does.

  1. Collects vitals from a simulated Astroskin wearable: body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure (systolic/diastolic), blood glucose, sleep hours, and self-reported mood (1–5 scale).
  2. Evaluates each indicator against evidence-based thresholds (sourced from NASA HRP, OCHMO technical briefs, ADA, AHA, CDC, MedlinePlus). Every reading returns a state + direction: { state: 'yellow', direction: 'high' } → maps to a specific message and action.
  3. Explains in plain language. No diagnosis. Instead of “you have an infection,” the app says “this may be the start of a fever — rest, drink water, measure again in 30 minutes.”
  4. Adapts to habitat context. The user selects their current habitat (ISS, Mars transit, Moon base, Mars base). Each habitat carries its own radiation accumulation rate (based on Curiosity RAD measurements and ISS data), gravity level, and Earth-communication delay. Red-state protocols include habitat-specific lines (e.g., “You are in maximum autonomy. Follow the protocol while the response arrives” for Mars).
  5. AI assistant (the “H.A.L.O.” voice). A serverless proxy (Vercel Function) calls an LLM that receives the current vitals + habitat state and returns a contextualized briefing — connecting, e.g., a high heart rate on Mars transit with cumulative radiation exposure and dehydration risk. The proxy keeps the API key off the client.
  6. Earth alerts. Red states trigger a simulated transmission to ground: “Alert sent to Earth. Estimated response in {delay}. Follow the protocol meanwhile.” A wrist-watch style alert on the UI mirrors this.
  7. Routine reminders. Each measurement is timestamped (localStorage). If an indicator is overdue (e.g., no temperature logged in 24 h), the app prompts the astronaut on reopening.

Technical stack. Pure HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend, deployed on Vercel. One Vercel serverless function (/api/asistente) proxies the AI assistant calls. No backend database — all state lives in the browser via localStorage for the hackathon prototype, which keeps the system testable offline and easy to port into a real flight-software environment.

Why it matters. The solution lowers the medical-expertise ceiling on long missions: any crew member can interpret their own numbers, act on them in the first critical minutes, and keep Earth in the loop without waiting on a round-trip. The habitat model makes the same tool portable from ISS to Mars with only a configuration change — the protocols shift automatically with the communication delay and radiation environment.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

This project used AI in two distinct roles.

(1) AI as a product feature. H.A.L.O. integrates a large-language-model assistant that correlates the astronaut’s current vitals with their habitat context (radiation exposure, gravity, isolation duration) to give a non-clinician a human-readable briefing and next-action guidance. The LLM is called through a Vercel serverless function that keeps API credentials off the client. Guardrails: the assistant never diagnoses; it orients. Thresholds and clinical messages come from NASA / medical sources (see References), not from the model.

(2) AI as a development tool. Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout the 48 hours as a pair-programming and research assistant to accelerate the indicator-thresholds research, draft and review JavaScript modules, and translate NASA source material into plain-language user-facing copy. All thresholds, sources, and clinical content were verified by the team against the original NASA / ADA / AHA / CDC / MedlinePlus documents before inclusion.
